newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore committee reports on costs controversy.
newsitem.headline: Singapore committee reports on costs controversy.

text.p: Singapore's Cost Review Committee on Friday summed up its case that costs are not rising as sharply as opposition politicians have claimed.

The issue has been a key one in Singapore politics in recent months, and four opposition figures face possible fines and jail terms on charges they committed contempt of parliament in testimony before another committee reviewing health care costs.

Members of the government-appointed Cost Review Committee said at a news conference that Singaporeans' spending rose by 76 percent in the five years to fiscal 1992/1993 (April-March), but actual price increases accounted for only 14 percentage points of the total.
Members said the remaining 62 percentage point rise was due to "other factors", particularly lifestyle changes resulting in purchases of better-quality food, clothing and appliances.

The committee, formed in 1992, was reconvened in July after the opposition Singapore Democratic Party (SDP) and Singapore Malay National Organisation said cost rises in recent years had been "no less than phenomenal" and accounted for most of the increase in household spending during the five-year period.

At the news conference, the committee said that between 1992 and 1995, hospital fees rose only 4.4 percent annually, public transport costs less than 2.0 percent, and university fees only 3.7 percent. Public housing rose more sharply, by between 5.4 percent and 11 percent a year.
"The increases are also due to an increase in wages," said committee Chairman Lim Boon Heng. "The increases have not been as alarming and not as high as it is made up to be."
Lim did not say how much wages had risen.
Opposition figures had met with the committee and also testified before the Select Committee on Health Care that specifically looked at the issue of health-care costs.

The SDP told the latter that government health spending had dipped to just five percent of total outlay from some 40 percent 20 years earlier. It later admitted the five percent figure was wrong and should have been 25.4 percent.

That became a central issue in charges that SDP Secretary-General Chee Soon Juan and three colleagues deliberately misled the committee and were in contempt of parliament. They have denied the charges.
